original_value: Thermal characteristic analysis is essential for machine tool spindles because sudden failures may occur due to unexpected thermal issue. This article presents a lumped-parameter Thermal Network Model (TNM) and its parameter estimation scheme, including hardware and software, in order to characterize both the steady-state and transient thermal behavior of machine tool spindles. For the hardware, the authors develop a Bluetooth Temperature Sensor Module (BTSM) which accompanying with three types of temperature-sensing probes (magnetic, screw, and probe). Its specification, through experimental test, achieves to the precision ±(0.1 + 0.0029|t|) °C, resolution 0.00489 °C, power consumption 7 mW, and size Ø40 mm × 27 mm. For the software, the heat transfer characteristics of the machine tool spindle correlative to rotating speed are derived based on the theory of heat transfer and empirical formula. The predictive TNM of spindles was developed by grey-box estimation and experimental results. Even under such complicated operating conditions as various speeds and different initial conditions, the experiments validate that the present modeling methodology provides a robust and reliable tool for the temperature prediction with normalized mean square error of 99.5% agreement, and the present approach is transferable to the other spindles with a similar structure. For realizing the edge computing in smart manufacturing, a reduced-order TNM is constructed by Model Order Reduction (MOR) technique and implemented into the real-time embedded system.

result.paraphrase: Thermal analysis is crucial for machine tool spindles, since unexpected thermal problems can lead to sudden failures. This article introduces a lumped-parameter Thermal Network Model (TNM) and a parameter-estimation framework, covering both hardware and software, to describe the steady-state and transient thermal behavior of machine tool spindles. On the hardware side, the authors created a Bluetooth Temperature Sensor Module (BTSM) with three kinds of temperature-sensing probes: magnetic, screw, and probe. Experimental testing shows a precision of ±(0.1 + 0.0029|t|) °C, a resolution of 0.00489 °C, power consumption of 7 mW, and dimensions of Ø40 mm × 27 mm. On the software side, the spindle heat-transfer characteristics related to rotating speed are derived from heat-transfer theory and empirical formulas. The predictive spindle TNM is developed through grey-box estimation and experimental results. Even under complex operating conditions with varying speeds and different initial conditions, the experiments confirm that the modeling method is a robust and reliable temperature-prediction tool, with normalized mean square error showing 99.5% agreement, and that the approach can be transferred to other spindles with similar structures. To support edge computing in smart manufacturing, a reduced-order TNM is built using Model Order Reduction (MOR) and implemented in a real-time embedded system.
